End-of-Support OS on Customer SFTP File.asset: Customer payroll files (employee names, national ID numbers, bank account details and pay data) held on the two customer SFTP servers, Asset-412 and Asset-413
End-of-Support OS on Customer SFTP File.threat_community: External cybercriminals who can reach the servers, including through allowlisted customer networks
End-of-Support OS on Customer SFTP File.condition: Both SFTP (Secure File Transfer Protocol) servers run an operating system that reached end of support in January 2026. It gets no security patches, so any newly disclosed flaw stays open. The firewall allowlist also includes several broad /16 ranges, and no SIEM alert rules exist for these servers. Migration to the managed file transfer platform is planned but not funded this quarter.

controls.control: Firewall allowlist limits inbound connections to registered customer IP ranges (several are broad /16 blocks)
Key-based authentication only
controls.note: Stops password guessing, but does not stop pre-authentication exploits, and a stolen customer key still gives a login.

controls.control: Files purged 7 days after pickup
OS and SFTP logs forwarded to the SIEM (security information and event management), with no alert rules specific to these servers
controls.note: Logs are collected, but with no alert rules for these servers nobody is told in time to limit the loss.

End-of-Support OS on Customer SFTP File.scenario_sentence: External cybercriminals cause loss of confidentiality to customer payroll files on the two customer SFTP servers through exploiting unpatched operating system flaws, reached from allowlisted ranges, with stolen customer keys, or by lateral movement from an internal foothold.
notes: Assumed the default scenario covers all three exploit paths in the entry, since they share the same asset, threat community and effect.
Assumed the lateral movement path (3) is carried out by an external attacker who already has an internal foothold, not by a malicious insider.
The entry says a compromise exposes every customer's files on disk at that time. The amount on disk depends on the 7-day purge window and upload volume, which the entry does not give.
The entry says about 340 customers upload files, but not how many have files on disk at any one time.
Assumed the SIEM logs help with detection after the fact only, so they are marked as not reducing loss until alert rules exist.
Open question: do management ports on these servers have any extra restrictions, such as a separate network zone or an administrative jump host? The entry does not say.
Open question: is there any evidence of past attempts or compromise on these servers since January 2026?
The planned interim steps (narrower allowlist, SIEM alert rules, 3-day purge) are not treated as baseline controls here.

alternatives.title: Stolen customer key used to escalate privileges and read other customers' folders
alternatives.asset: Other customers' payroll files on the SFTP servers, reached from one customer's login
alternatives.threat_community: External cybercriminals holding a stolen customer SFTP key
alternatives.reason: Narrowing allowlist ranges does little here because the attacker uses a valid key. Key rotation or per-customer isolation would matter more. A shorter purge window and SIEM alerts would affect this path differently from remote exploit.

No MFA on Legacy Support Admin Console.asset: Customer tenant data held in the legacy support admin console (Asset-118, Nova environment), including the ability to view and change it
No MFA on Legacy Support Admin Console.threat_community: External attackers using stolen or guessed support engineer credentials
No MFA on Legacy Support Admin Console.condition: The legacy support admin console signs in with username and password only. It is not connected to corporate single sign-on (SSO), so multi-factor authentication (MFA) is not enforced. About 220 support engineers use it, and 35 accounts can impersonate any customer administrator.

controls.control: Console reachable only from the corporate network or VPN (VPN requires MFA)
12-character passwords with 90-day rotation
Account lockout after 10 failed attempts
Console activity logs retained for 90 days and reviewed only on request
controls.note: Logs are reviewed only on request, so they do not stop or limit an attack in progress. They only support later investigation.

controls.control: Quarterly access recertification

No MFA on Legacy Support Admin Console.scenario_sentence: External attackers using stolen or guessed support engineer credentials cause loss of confidentiality to customer tenant data in the legacy support admin console through logging in with phished, sprayed or reused passwords from a compromised corporate endpoint, an active VPN session or an internal foothold.
notes: Assumed the default effect is confidentiality because the risk statement leads with viewing customer tenant data. Changing data (integrity) is treated as a secondary effect.
Assumed the attacker first gains a foothold on the corporate network or VPN, since the console is not reachable from outside. The entry does not say how likely that step is.
Password reuse from third-party breaches (path 3) still needs network access to the console. The entry does not say whether this path depends on the same foothold.
The entry does not say how many customer tenants or records are exposed, or whether tenant data is encrypted. Please confirm for magnitude.
Lockout at 10 failed attempts is assumed to be per account, which is why password spraying can stay under it.
Logs are kept 90 days and reviewed only on request. Assumed there is no active detection today, since alerting on impersonation events is only in the mitigation plan.
The 6% phishing simulation click rate is noted as context for susceptibility to phishing. It is not a control.
Mitigation plan (SSO, MFA, disabling local login, impersonation alerting) is not treated as a baseline control.

alternatives.title: Malicious change of customer tenant data via impersonation
alternatives.asset: Customer tenant configuration and data changeable through the 35 impersonation-capable accounts
alternatives.threat_community: External attackers using stolen credentials of impersonation-privileged accounts
alternatives.reason: Acting as a customer administrator lets an attacker change data, not just read it. This is a different effect with different losses, such as restoring tenants and customer disputes.

alternatives.title: Impersonation-privileged accounts versus ordinary support accounts
alternatives.asset: Customer tenant data reachable through the 35 impersonation-privileged accounts
alternatives.threat_community: External attackers using stolen credentials of impersonation-privileged accounts
alternatives.reason: The plan adds alerting on tenant impersonation events, which affects only the 35 privileged accounts. MFA and SSO apply to all 220 users. Splitting lets the analyst measure each mitigation separately.

Over-Privileged CI/CD Deployment Role in.asset: Production data and infrastructure in the Granite production cloud account (Asset-907, Asset-355)
Over-Privileged CI/CD Deployment Role in.threat_community: External attackers who compromise the build pipeline, its engineer accounts, its access keys or a third-party build dependency
Over-Privileged CI/CD Deployment Role in.condition: The deployment role used by the CI/CD (continuous integration and continuous delivery) pipeline has wildcard administrative permissions instead of deployment-scoped permissions. It uses long-lived access keys stored as pipeline variables, last rotated 14 months ago. About 60 engineers can edit pipeline definitions, and one reviewer is enough to approve a change. The posture tool has flagged the finding as high severity for 5 months without a fix.

controls.control: Pipeline changes require a pull request with one reviewer
Cloud audit logging is enabled and forwarded to the SIEM (security information and event management system)
controls.note: Logging does not block access. It helps detect misuse and shorten the time the attacker has, which limits how much is lost.

controls.control: The production account is separate from development and test accounts
controls.note: The role is over-privileged inside the production account itself, so the separation does not limit what the attacker can reach in this scenario.

controls.control: The posture tool scans daily
controls.note: The tool has flagged this finding for 5 months with no fix. It detects the weakness but does not reduce attacker success or loss.

Over-Privileged CI/CD Deployment Role in.scenario_sentence: External attackers cause loss of confidentiality to production data and infrastructure in the Granite production cloud account through use of the over-privileged CI/CD deployment role after compromising the pipeline, its access keys or a third-party build dependency.
notes: Assumed the default effect is confidentiality because the risk statement lists reading data first. The entry also names changing and destroying data, which would be integrity and availability losses.
Assumed Asset-907 and Asset-355 are the production data and infrastructure reachable by the deployment role. The entry does not describe them.
The entry does not say what data is held in the production account or how sensitive it is. This is needed to estimate loss magnitude.
Exploit path 1 may start with a malicious engineer. Treated here as an attacker using a compromised engineer account. A true insider would be a different threat community.
The entry does not say whether the SIEM has alerts for deployment role activity, or how fast anyone would respond.
The entry does not say whether the access keys have been seen in build logs or leaked before.
Assumed the mitigation plan is not yet in place, so all baseline controls are as described.

alternatives.title: Attacker destroys or alters production infrastructure and data using the deployment role
alternatives.asset: Production infrastructure and data integrity in the Granite production cloud account
alternatives.threat_community: External attackers who compromise the build pipeline or its credentials
alternatives.reason: Deleting or changing infrastructure causes outage and recovery costs, not data exposure. The loss types and the response differ from the confidentiality scenario, so they should be sized separately.

alternatives.title: Malicious engineer abuses pipeline edit access to run commands as the deployment role
alternatives.asset: Production data and infrastructure in the Granite production cloud account
alternatives.threat_community: Malicious insiders among the roughly 60 engineers who can edit pipeline definitions
alternatives.reason: An insider has legitimate access and knows the system. The threat type, how often it happens and how well the one-reviewer check works all differ from an outside attacker.

alternatives.title: Leaked pipeline access keys are used directly from outside the pipeline
alternatives.asset: Production data and infrastructure in the Granite production cloud account
alternatives.threat_community: External attackers who obtain leaked long-lived access keys
alternatives.reason: Moving to short-lived federated credentials mainly stops this path. The reviewer rule on pipeline changes does not affect it, so the mitigations hit the paths differently.

User Access Reviews Not Performed for Pa.asset: Payroll data in the payroll processing application (Asset-562), covering about 480 internal user accounts' access to view and change payroll records
User Access Reviews Not Performed for Pa.threat_community: Users with stale access (people who changed roles and former contractors) and attackers who take over their dormant accounts
User Access Reviews Not Performed for Pa.condition: Quarterly user access reviews were not done for Q1 and Q2 2026 because the application owner role was vacant. A spot check of 50 accounts found 7 role changers and 2 terminated contractors who still had access. 30 local accounts sit outside single sign-on (SSO), so HR-driven deprovisioning and multi-factor authentication (MFA) do not cover them.

controls.control: SSO with MFA for all accounts except the 30 local accounts
controls.note: Does not cover the 30 local accounts. It also does not stop a user whose access is still active and approved.

controls.control: HR-driven deprovisioning of SSO accounts on termination
controls.note: Covers leavers on SSO only. It does not catch role changers, contractors missed by HR, or the 30 local accounts.

controls.control: Role-based access inside the application
controls.note: Limits what each role can see, but stale roles from previous jobs still grant access to payroll data.

controls.control: Application audit log records payroll changes
controls.note: Records changes only, so it may not show who viewed data. It helps detect and investigate after the event rather than prevent it.

User Access Reviews Not Performed for Pa.scenario_sentence: Users with stale access, or attackers who take over their dormant accounts, cause loss of confidentiality to payroll data in the payroll processing application through access that was never removed because reviews were not done.
notes: Assumed the default scenario is unauthorized viewing of payroll data (confidentiality) by people with stale access, as the risk statement lists viewing first.
Assumed stale-access users acting on their own are the main threat community, and that account takeover of dormant accounts is a path within the same scenario.
The entry does not say whether the audit log records read access. This matters for detecting unauthorized viewing.
The entry does not say what the payroll data includes (for example bank details or national ID numbers). Please confirm, as this affects loss magnitude.
The spot check found 9 of 50 accounts (18%) with unneeded access. It is unknown whether this rate applies to all 480 accounts.
It is unknown whether any of the stale accounts were actually used to view or change data. Audit log review could show this.
Assumed MFA is enforced for all SSO accounts as the entry states.
The likely SOC 2 (System and Organization Controls 2) audit exception is a compliance matter. Any related losses such as audit findings or customer impact are not scoped here.

alternatives.title: Stale access users change payroll data without authorization
alternatives.asset: Integrity of payroll records in the payroll processing application (Asset-562)
alternatives.threat_community: Users with stale access, including role changers and terminated contractors
alternatives.reason: Changing payroll data (for example pay or bank details) is a different effect from viewing it. Losses such as fraudulent payments and corrections differ from those of a data exposure.

alternatives.title: Takeover of the 30 local accounts outside SSO
alternatives.asset: Payroll data in the payroll processing application (Asset-562)
alternatives.threat_community: External cybercriminals taking over dormant local accounts
alternatives.reason: The plan to migrate or remove the 30 local accounts affects this path differently from the access review of all 480 accounts. These accounts also lack MFA and HR deprovisioning, so the threat and controls differ.

Unsupported Insecure Protocol on Third-P.asset: Customer employee data (names, dates of birth, dependents and benefit elections) exchanged with the third-party benefits provider through the legacy integration (Asset-274, Asset-690)
Unsupported Insecure Protocol on Third-P.threat_community: External attackers on the network path or holding the shared integration credential
Unsupported Insecure Protocol on Third-P.condition: The benefits integration uses a legacy SOAP (Simple Object Access Protocol) API over TLS 1.0 with basic authentication and one shared service account. The provider no longer supports this API version and issues no security fixes for it.

controls.control: Firewall rules restrict integration traffic to the provider's IP ranges
Web application firewall (WAF) on the product's public endpoints
controls.note: It does not inspect outbound server-to-server integration traffic, so it does not reduce loss here.

controls.control: Integration requests are logged
Only authenticated, authorized customer users can trigger the integration
controls.note: It limits who can start the integration from the product. It does not stop network interception or use of the stolen shared credential directly against the provider.

Unsupported Insecure Protocol on Third-P.scenario_sentence: External attackers cause loss of confidentiality to customer employee data exchanged with the third-party benefits provider through interception of the TLS 1.0 session or theft and misuse of the shared basic-authentication credential.
notes: Assumed the default scenario is confidentiality only, covering paths 1 and 2. Tampering in path 1 is an integrity effect and is not covered here.
Assumed an attacker on the network path is able to break or downgrade TLS 1.0. The entry does not say how likely this is.
The entry does not say where the shared credential is stored or who can read the configuration. Please confirm.
The firewall allowlist limits who can reach the provider from the product. It is unclear whether it limits where the stolen credential can be used against the provider.
Logging is assumed to help with detection and scoping after an event. The entry does not say if anyone reviews the logs or if alerts exist today.
About 1,100 customers use the feature. Please confirm how much data could be exposed in one event.
The provider has given no firm retirement date for the legacy API. This affects the path 3 timing.

alternatives.title: Provider retires legacy API and benefits feature stops
alternatives.asset: Availability of the benefits enrollment feature for about 1,100 customers
alternatives.reason: This path is not malicious and causes loss of availability, not loss of confidentiality. It needs its own frequency and loss estimates, such as support cost and customer impact.

alternatives.title: Tampering with benefit data in transit
alternatives.asset: Integrity of benefit elections and employee data exchanged with the provider
alternatives.threat_community: External attackers on the network path
alternatives.reason: Tampering corrupts data instead of exposing it. The loss types differ, such as correcting wrong enrollments, so it needs a separate estimate.

No Data Loss Prevention on Workstations.asset: Customer data extracts downloaded to the 85 data engineer and support analyst workstations (Asset-731, Nova environment)
No Data Loss Prevention on Workstations.threat_community: Employees and contractors with workstation access to customer data extracts, including malware running under their accounts
No Data Loss Prevention on Workstations.condition: The 85 workstations have no Data Loss Prevention (DLP) agent or egress monitoring. USB mass storage and personal cloud storage are not blocked. Extracts are not tracked after download and no retention limit is enforced, so old extracts stay on workstations (9 of 20 sampled had extracts older than 90 days).

controls.control: Full-disk encryption on all workstations
controls.note: Encryption protects data at rest if a device is lost or stolen. It does not stop a logged-in user or malware from copying files to USB or cloud storage.

controls.control: EDR (endpoint detection and response) agent on all workstations
controls.note: May detect malware activity, but it is not built to spot a user copying extracts to USB or cloud storage.

controls.control: Acceptable use policy and annual training
controls.note: Discourages deliberate or careless copying but does not technically prevent it.

controls.control: Extract requests require ticket approval
controls.note: Limits who can get extracts and leaves a record of requests, but does not control what happens after download.

controls.control: Web proxy logs retained for 30 days
controls.note: Supports after-the-fact detection and investigation of uploads through the proxy. It does not prevent copying and does not cover USB.

No Data Loss Prevention on Workstations.scenario_sentence: Employees and contractors with workstation access to customer data extracts, including malware running under their accounts, cause loss of confidentiality to customer data extracts on the 85 workstations through copying to personal cloud storage or removable media.
notes: Assumed the default is the insider path (employee or contractor acting on purpose), with malware on the workstation as a second path to the same loss.
Open question: is the insider copying deliberate or accidental? The risk statement does not say. Deliberate misuse is assumed.
Open question: how many customer records are in a typical extract, and do they include sensitive fields? The entry does not say.
Open question: does the EDR agent have any device control or upload monitoring features turned on?
Assumed the web proxy covers traffic from these workstations to cloud storage sites, but not off-network use or USB.
Assumed the 2025 audit finding (old extracts on 9 of 20 workstations) raises the amount of data exposed per event, not how often events occur.
The register entry does not say whether any past copying incidents have occurred.

alternatives.title: Malware on workstation exfiltrates stored extracts
alternatives.asset: Customer data extracts stored on the 85 workstations
alternatives.threat_community: External cybercriminals running malware on a workstation
alternatives.reason: The actor is external, not an insider. EDR matters much more here, and the likelihood and attack steps differ from deliberate insider copying.

alternatives.title: Employee accidentally leaves extracts on workstations past retention
alternatives.asset: Customer data extracts older than 90 days on workstations
alternatives.reason: The planned move to a controlled analysis environment removes local extracts, which fixes this path. DLP and USB blocking mainly address deliberate copying, so the mitigations affect the paths differently.

Backup Restoration Untested for Time and.asset: Time and attendance production database (Asset-208, about 6 TB, Granite environment) and its availability to about 2,300 customers who use it for timekeeping that feeds payroll
Backup Restoration Untested for Time and.threat_community: Mixed causes of data loss: database corruption from a failed change or system fault, and ransomware actors, affecting the backup and recovery process
Backup Restoration Untested for Time and.condition: No full restore test has been run in 19 months. The last test predates a major schema change and a storage migration. The real restore time for the 6 TB database is unknown, so the team cannot show it can meet the 8-hour recovery time objective.

controls.control: Nightly full and hourly log backups to a separate storage account
Backup job monitoring with alerts on failure
controls.note: It catches failed backup jobs. It does not show whether a restore works or how long it takes, so it only partly reduces the loss.

controls.control: Immutable backup copies retained for 30 days
Database replicated to a secondary region
controls.note: Replication would also copy logical corruption, so it does not help recover from corruption or a bad change. It may help only with a regional outage, which the entry does not describe.

Backup Restoration Untested for Time and.scenario_sentence: A data-loss event on the time and attendance database (corruption, failed change or ransomware) causes loss of availability to the time and attendance production database through a restore that cannot finish within the 8-hour recovery time objective.
notes: Assumed the default scenario is loss of availability from a slow or failed restore, not a breach of confidentiality, even though ransomware is one trigger.
Assumed threat type is Failure (system or vendor), since the entry lists corruption and a failed change alongside ransomware. The analyst may prefer to split ransomware out.
The actual restore time is unknown. Open question: what is a reasonable estimate for a 6 TB restore on the migrated storage?
Open question: has the restore procedure been checked against the new schema and storage after the migration?
Assumed SLA credits apply when the 8-hour objective is missed. The entry does not give credit amounts or contract terms.
Assumed the 24-hour recovery point objective is met by the hourly log backups. The entry does not confirm this.
The entry does not say how often corruption, failed changes or ransomware events have occurred, so frequency needs to be estimated.
Open question: is the immutable copy a full backup that can be restored on its own, and has it been tested?

alternatives.title: Ransomware encrypts the time and attendance database and backups are needed
alternatives.reason: Ransomware is a deliberate external attack, while the default covers accidental failures. Frequency and controls differ. Immutable backups matter most here, and the attacker may also try to reach backups.

alternatives.title: Logical corruption or failed change replicated to the secondary region
alternatives.threat_community: Internal staff making changes, and the database system
alternatives.reason: Replication copies bad data, so only backups and restore tests help. The restore test mitigation affects this path more than the ransomware path, where immutable copies already help.

Hardcoded Secrets in Source Code Reposit.asset: Production database contents and third-party service data (payments and messaging providers) reachable with the 212 hardcoded secrets in 41 source code repositories (Asset-846, Asset-129)
Hardcoded Secrets in Source Code Reposit.threat_community: external attackers who take over a developer or contractor account with repository access
Hardcoded Secrets in Source Code Reposit.condition: 212 secrets, including 18 production database credentials and 9 third-party API keys, are hardcoded in 41 repositories and many have never been rotated. Use of the central vault is voluntary. There is no pre-commit or push-time secret scanning, and the only check is a manual scan each quarter. About 1,900 engineers and 150 contractors can read the repositories.

controls.control: Repositories are private and require single sign-on (SSO) with multi-factor authentication (MFA)
Production databases are reachable only from production network segments
controls.note: Limits direct use of database credentials from outside. It does not help against third-party API keys, which work from the internet, or against an attacker already inside the production network.

controls.control: Central secrets vault exists but use is voluntary
controls.note: The 212 secrets are still in the code, so the vault does not reduce loss until secrets are moved into it.

controls.control: Manual secret scan run quarterly
controls.note: It finds secrets after the fact and does not stop them being committed. Old secrets stayed in history unrotated for over two years, so it has not reduced exposure.

Hardcoded Secrets in Source Code Reposit.scenario_sentence: External attackers who take over a developer or contractor account cause loss of confidentiality to production database contents and third-party service data through harvesting hardcoded secrets from source code repositories and using them to access those systems.
notes: Assumed the default scenario covers the attacker path where an account is compromised and secrets are harvested, then used against both databases and third-party services.
The entry does not say what data the production databases or the payments and messaging providers hold. The records and volume at stake are an open question.
The entry does not say if any secret has already been misused. Evidence of past misuse would change how often the threat acts.
Assumed Asset-846 and Asset-129 are the repository or system assets linked to this risk. The entry does not say which is which.
The entry does not say if secrets are shared across repositories or environments. If so, one stolen secret could expose more.
The entry does not say how the 1,900 engineers and 150 contractors are protected beyond SSO and MFA. For example, device checks and session limits are not mentioned.
The mitigation plan (rotation, vault, push-time scanning) is not yet in place and is not counted as a baseline control.

alternatives.asset: Production databases holding the 18 exposed credentials
alternatives.threat_community: malicious insiders or attackers with a foothold in the production network

alternatives.threat_community: external attackers using stolen API keys from the internet
alternatives.reason: Sending fraudulent messages or payment actions harms integrity, not only confidentiality. No network restriction applies, so controls and losses differ from the database path.

Overdue Security Assessment for Support.threat_community: external attackers who breach the support ticketing vendor or its sub-processors
Overdue Security Assessment for Support.condition: The vendor's security assessment is 14 months overdue. controls.note: This protects against stolen agent credentials. It does not protect against a breach inside the vendor's own environment or sub-processors.

controls.control: The vendor is on the critical vendor list
controls.note: This is a classification only. It does not reduce loss unless it leads to oversight, and the assessment is overdue.

controls.control: Annual assessment is required by policy (currently not met)
controls.note: The requirement is not being met, so it is not reducing loss now.

Overdue Security Assessment for Support.scenario_sentence: External attackers cause loss of confidentiality to customer PII held in the support ticketing vendor's tickets and attachments through a breach of the vendor or its sub-processors that goes unnoticed because of weak vendor oversight.

Assumed the vendor's own controls are unknown until the overdue assessment and current SOC 2 report are done.
The planned 12-month attachment retention limit would reduce how much data is exposed. It is not yet in place, so it is not counted as a baseline control.

paths.title: Insider copies extracts to removable media

steps.text: Employee or contractor with an approved extract request downloads customer data extracts to their workstation.

paths.title: Restore takes longer than the 8-hour objective

steps.text: Corruption, a failed change or a system fault makes the production database unusable.
controls: Backup job monitoring with alerts on failure

steps.text: The team decides to restore from backup and starts a full restore of the roughly 6 TB database.
controls: Nightly full and hourly log backups to a separate storage account

steps.text: The restore runs on the migrated storage. Its real speed has never been measured, so it is slower than planned.
The restore and log replay pass the 8-hour objective while about 2,300 customers cannot record time that feeds payroll.
The outage is extended, SLA credits apply and customers lose trust.

paths.what_fails: The restore time was never measured on the current database size and storage, so the 8-hour objective cannot be shown to be met.
makes_worse: Restore happens near payroll deadlines
Log replay adds many hours to the restore
Staff are unfamiliar with the restore steps
Storage throughput in the new setup is lower than expected
limits: Hourly log backups keep data loss within the 24-hour recovery point objective
Nightly backups sit in a separate storage account

paths.title: Restore procedure fails after schema change and storage migration

steps.text: The database needs recovery after corruption or a bad change.
The team follows a restore procedure last tested before the major schema change and storage migration.

The first restore attempt fails or produces a database that does not work. The team has to troubleshoot while the service is down.
controls: Backup job monitoring with alerts on failure

steps.text: The retry and fixes push recovery well past 8 hours, causing extended customer outage and SLA credits.

paths.title: Replicated corruption leaves backups as the only recovery route

steps.text: A failed change or system fault damages data in the production database.
Replication copies the damage to the secondary region, so failover does not give a clean copy.
The team must restore from backup and choose a point in time before the damage.
controls: Nightly full and hourly log backups to a separate storage account
Immutable backup copies retained for 30 days

steps.text: The team finds the backups have not been tested for restore time or completeness. The chosen backup may be slow to restore or not usable on its own.
Recovery runs past the 8-hour objective and customers lose timekeeping availability.

paths.what_fails: Replication offers no protection against logical corruption, and backup restores are untested.
makes_worse: Damage goes unnoticed for days, so the clean restore point is old
Immutable copy is not a full backup and needs extra steps to restore
limits: Immutable copies kept for 30 days give older clean restore points
Hourly log backups allow a restore to a point just before the damage
